en: The *Sūtra on the Ganges River* Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakara of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, various disciples, and bodhisattvas.
They arrived at the Ganges River.

Countless devas, humans, spirits, nāgas, humans and non-humans, as well as those who had first resolved their minds toward the Way, each holding flowers, incense, and musical instruments, all followed after the Buddha. Having reached the Ganges, he prepared a seat and sat down; the entire assembly became settled in concentration.

On the fifteenth day of the month, during the recitation of the precepts, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, stepped forward to pay homage, and touched his head to the Buddha’s feet. He then knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The disciples are seated in tranquility; I pray that the Buddha will authorize the recitation of the Sūtra of Precepts.”
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond; Ānanda returned to his seat for a very long time.
At midnight, Ānanda rose again, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Midnight has arrived, and all the disciples are settled in their seats; I pray that you will grant us the opportunity to hear the Buddha recite the Sūtra on the Precepts."
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond; Ānanda returned to his seat for a very long time.
As the roosters were about to crow, Ānanda rose again, knelt before the Buddha with palms joined, and said to him:
“The roosters are about to crow; the disciples wish to hear the Buddha recite the Sūtra of the Precepts.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Human beings revolve through the five realms of existence, coming and going; their suffering in this world is immense. That they do not recognize the beginning and end of their own past lives is entirely due to the lack of rectitude in their minds."

A human body is extremely difficult to obtain; having obtained a human body, it is further difficult to encounter and hear the Buddha’s sutras and precepts; having heard the Buddha’s sutras and precepts, it is again difficult to believe and enter the Buddha-way; and having entered the Buddha-way, it is once more difficult to maintain and uphold the sutras and precepts.

The Buddha wished to recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, but there was now a disciple among those seated here who could not uphold the Buddha’s Prātimokṣa Sūtra; for this reason, the Buddha did not recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “I do not know which disciple does not uphold the Buddha’s Sūtra on the Precepts.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having seen through with his samādhi, perceived the disciple who did not uphold the precepts; he immediately rose and went before him, saying to him:

“You have become a disciple of the Buddha, yet you are unable to uphold the precepts. You are a person who has cast aside the Dharma; you should not share a seat with the Venerable One. You must rise and depart; you are no longer permitted to remain among the assembly.”
The Buddha said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“You must skillfully instruct and cause those disciples who do not uphold the precepts to leave.
Thereupon, they felt ashamed and departed.
The Buddha addressed his disciples:
"Listen well as I now preach the Dharma.
All the disciples joined their palms and said:
“Yes, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said:
“The waters of the great ocean come and go at dawn and dusk, yet they never exceed their established boundaries; when they recede, they likewise do not exceed those same boundaries.”

All you disciples should straighten your hearts and rectify your intentions; look back within yourselves at the five internal organs, contemplate how birth and death are exceedingly arduous and painful, and you must uphold this Sūtra of Precepts without ever violating them.
Those who uphold the five precepts will return to the human world as people.
Those who uphold the ten wholesome paths of action will attain rebirth in the heavens.
Those who uphold the two hundred and fifty precepts may, in this present life, attain the Great Way of Nirvana as Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Buddhas.
Having attained a human body through the Way, one should uphold the sutras and precepts; even at the cost of death, one must not violate them by so much as a hair’s breadth.
It is like the waters of the ocean, which come and go with the tides yet never dare to overstep their ancient boundaries.
Within the ocean there are seven treasures. What are these seven treasures? First is white silver;

second is gold; third is coral; fourth is white pearls; fifth is musāragalva (cat's-eye); sixth is the moon-illumining pearl; and seventh is the maṇi jewel. These are the seven treasures of the ocean.
"Now, within the Buddha-way there are likewise seven treasures.
The Buddha said,
"The treasure of the Way is it."

First is the srotāpanna, second is the sakṛdāgāmin, third is the anāgāmin, fourth is the arhat, fifth is the pratyekabuddha, sixth is the bodhisattva who has resolved to deliver all beings, and seventh is the Buddha’s Great Path of Nirvāṇa; these are the seven treasures.

Those who wish to attain the treasure of the Path must all abandon lustful excess, anger, and delusion; by upholding the precepts, practicing diligence, and accumulating merit, they shall maintain inner and outer purity and self-restraint—such is the noble person of impermanence.
The waters of the ocean do not tolerate impurities; if there be a corpse, a place of filth and stench, or anything unclean, a swift wind blows it onto the shore.

Likewise, within the Way of the Buddha, those wicked people who are defiled and do not uphold the sutras and precepts are not tolerated; rather, those who violate the sutras and precepts are seized by the arm and cast out.
For example, there are four kinds of rats:
first, those in the rafters; second, those in the house; third, those in the wild fields; and fourth, those in the latrine.

The rats in the eaves cannot dwell on level ground; the rats on level ground cannot dwell in the eaves; the rats in the wild fields cannot dwell in human houses; the rats in human houses cannot dwell in the wild fields; and the rats in the latrines cannot leave the latrines, because they do not know that there is an abundance of grain in the granary.
Furthermore, there are four classes of people.
What are these four classes?
One class of people straightens their hearts and rectifies their intentions, upholds the precepts without transgression, and seeks the path of an Arhat.
The second class of people maintain the precepts and practice with diligence, desiring to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha.
The third class of people maintain the precepts, engage in study, clarify the sutras through wisdom, and, mindful of delivering all beings, desire to attain the path of a buddha.

The four classes of followers rely on the mere name of being disciples; they are unable to uphold the clear precepts and have no desire for study, as their minds are hesitant and fearful that they will not attain the Way.
"These are the disciples who come and go; such are the four classes of mice.
The Buddha said, "O disciples!"

In the world there are five rivers: one flowing east is named Śalukī; one flowing south is named Aciravatī; one flowing west is named Gaṅgā; one flowing north is named Yamunā; and the one flowing through the center is named Sindhu.
When they turn and flow into the ocean, they all discard their original names and become simply the waters of the sea.
The Buddha said: "Disciples!
There are those of the Brahmin caste, those of the Kṣatriya caste, those of the artisan caste, those of the agriculturalist caste, and there are beggars."
There are those of various sorts who each claim, saying:
"My lineage is noble and distinguished.

Just as one might feel shame regarding wealth and pleasure while being poor and lowly, so too shall it be when these various sorts become disciples of the Buddha; they must all discard their original names and titles to truly be disciples of this Buddha!
How could there be any further pride regarding status as noble or lowly?
One who knows first should instruct those who know later;
one must not say, "I know."
One should not be self-conceited or arrogant;
one must not say,
"I have studied for a long time and know many scriptures."
One must not say:
"What I intend to do is right, while what he does is wrong.
Those who do so all violate the precepts and shall not be permitted to enter the assembly.

In the Way and its Dharma, seniors and juniors should instruct and protect one another, and they must follow this succession. If there are those who do not yet understand the scriptures and the Way, one must not speak of profound matters to them; to do so would be a grave transgression.

When it rains heavily throughout the world, the water flows into the drainage ditches; the drainage ditches flow into the mountain streams; the mountain streams flow into the rivers; and the rivers flow into the great ocean. Yet the waters of the great ocean neither increase nor decrease.
"Disciples!

Among those who study the Way and attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, there are those who attain *sakṛdāgāmin* or *anāgāmin*, those who attain *arhat*, those who attain *pratyekabuddha*, those who attain *avaivartika*, and those who attain the path of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*. Whether they come or go, the Buddha-way neither increases nor decreases, just as the water of the ocean neither increases nor decreases."

The Buddha said: "In the ocean there are great fish: the first is four thousand li long; the second is eight thousand li long; the third is twelve thousand li long; the fourth is sixteen thousand li long; the fifth is twenty thousand li long; the sixth is twenty-four thousand li long; and the seventh is twenty-eight thousand li long."
If one studies without encountering an enlightened teacher, how can one know that the Great Way exists in the world?
If one travels by boat upon a mere puddle or spring-fed stream, how can one know that there are rivers and seas in the world?

The Buddha’s sutras are like the rivers and seas; all the scriptures of the world have emerged from them. These sutras are difficult to encounter again for hearing or seeing; you should take them up to recite and study, for only after many tens of billions of years will there be the precepts of the Buddha’s sutras once more.
While the sun, moon, and stars shall eventually undergo destruction, there shall never be a time when the precepts of the Buddha’s sutras are destroyed.
From this day forward, the Buddha will no longer preach the sutras or the precepts.

"The precepts in the Buddha’s sutras are extremely grave; for within them it is stated that anyone who receives and upholds the precepts yet commits evil shall have their head split into seven pieces.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all his disciples single-mindedly and reverently upheld the Dharma of the precepts. The devas, humans, ghosts, spirits, and nāgas all rose forward, touched their heads and faces to the ground, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ganges River
